title: The hypertrophy series: maintaining tonnage stability for long term progress
summary: Tonnage should rise steadily over time without big jumps. Adding too much volume at once (e.g. four sets of a new exercise) causes poor recovery, illness or overuse injury and turns people off volume. Add one or two sets of compounds, introduce new movements light, judge the effect across the week, and accept only small planned dips.

claims.claim: The goal of hypertrophy training is to increase tonnage over time, through intensity or volume; if you're progressing, tonnage should rise.
Many people add too much tonnage too fast and it backfires (they can't recover, get sick, or get overuse injuries), convincing them wrongly that volume training isn't for them.
Everyone needs volume, in different measures; he drives tonnage mainly with volume while others lean on intensity, but both must be applied to some extent.
Adding four sets of a brand-new exercise is a great way to exhaust yourself and undo your goal.
When adding a heavy compound without removing anything, start with one or two sets, e.g. one extra back-off set of 10 squats, to gauge what volume you can handle.
When introducing a new variation or accessory, use 3-4 sets but start with very light weight even if you can handle much more.
A new movement should stay specific and make other lifts stronger; jumping tonnage by 400-500 lbs that leads to plateaus is worse than starting with about +200 and slowly climbing to 400.

Extra tonnage on one day affects the rest of that session and later sessions; judge it by strength, performance four days later, sensations, soreness and visible results, and move it elsewhere if it doesn't work.
Tonnage progression should be stable and rising, never regressing; gifted people progress faster.
Small tonnage dips from alternating or non-static rep ranges are fine and build momentum, as long as an increase follows soon after.
Step loading can be used occasionally, but training entirely by step loading makes tonnage swing too much to be conducive to hypertrophy.
Keep a training log: over about three years you'll see tonnage climb far higher, reflecting the strength and work capacity that produce bigger muscles.
Tonnage is fully under your control; control the variables and you control your muscular gains.
